scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an overnight maintenance window, pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports
pings to pc2 (200.1.1.2) are 100% lost, and pc2 reports the same
toward pc1. Yet monitoring shows the router1<->router2 eBGP
session Established with prefixes exchanged, and pc1 can still
ping BOTH of router2's addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1).
Identify what is dropping the traffic.

injection.action: add an iptables FORWARD rule dropping all transit ICMP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule for protocol icmp sits in router2's FORWARD
  chain, so any ICMP packet router2 must FORWARD (pc1<->pc2 transit
  in either direction) is discarded at the firewall layer. Traffic
  addressed TO router2 itself traverses INPUT, not FORWARD, which
  is why pc1 can still ping 193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1. The BGP
  session is TCP, not ICMP, so it stays Established and all
  prefixes remain exchanged -- routing is completely healthy; the
  drop is purely at the packet-filter layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for ICMP on
  router2
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec:
Remove the DROP rule on router2 -- `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`.
Transit pings between pc1 and pc2 succeed again immediately; no routing or
BGP change is needed.

agent.diagnosis_text:
During the overnight maintenance window, a blanket iptables FORWARD DROP
rule for protocol 1 (ICMP) was inserted on router2:

  Chain FORWARD (policy ACCEPT)
  rule 1: DROP  prot 1  any->any  (6 packets / 504 bytes matched)

This rule silently discards every ICMP packet that router2 must *forward*
in transit — that is, any packet whose destination IP is not router2 itself.
It does not touch the INPUT chain, which is why pings to router2's own
addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1) succeed: those packets are delivered
locally and never reach FORWARD. BGP traffic is likewise unaffected because
the TCP-179 session terminates on router2's INPUT chain. The eBGP session
therefore stays Established and prefixes continue to be exchanged, giving a
deceptive appearance of a healthy control plane while the data plane is
broken.

When pc1 (195.11.14.2) pings pc2 (200.1.1.2), the ICMP echo-request arrives
at router2 over eth0 and must be forwarded to eth1; the FORWARD rule drops it
before it reaches pc2 (confirmed: pc2 RX counter stayed at 0, and router2
itself can ping pc2 cleanly from its OUTPUT chain). The echo-reply path would
be symmetrically dropped as well.

Root cause: an erroneous `iptables -A FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` rule was added
to router2 during the maintenance window.

Corrective fix: remove the rule on router2:
  iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP
(or equivalently: iptables -D FORWARD 1)
To persist the correction across reboots, also remove the rule from any
iptables-save dump referenced by the startup configuration.
